Only a closure declared `throws` can throw into the catch, and it must be called as `try callback(...)`, so Swift makes the hazard visible at the call; the other side is that it is still writable, and a narrow port could flag it (0 sites today).

A Swift parameter is a constant, and data types are values, so changing a caller's data takes `inout` and an `&` at the call site; a class reached through a parameter is a reference whose mutation is its API, the host-object case this rule exempts.

Swift has no `in` operator, a Dictionary subscript is its real API, a Set has no key subscript and there is no `Object.keys`; the one shape that still compiles, `count < 0`, has 0 sites, which is the case for a small port.
